body:
Global space startups raised a record $20.8 billion (approximately NT$670 billion) in private funding in the third quarter of 2026 — nearly triple the previous quarter's $7.4 billion and more than double the prior all-time peak. The flood of capital concentrated heavily on launch services, satellite manufacturing, and orbital infrastructure, standing in sharp contrast to the weak share prices of publicly listed space companies. The "scissor gap" between primary-market frenzy and secondary-market valuation digestion has become the most closely watched core tension in the space industry.

According to a quarterly report released Wednesday by global investment firm Seraphim, even excluding Blue Origin's massive $10 billion raise, third-quarter space startup investment still reached $10.8 billion — a record high. The quarter saw 216 deals completed, also a new record and far above the 140 deals in the second quarter.

Primary market: Infrastructure dominates, sovereign demand emerges as a new driver

Infrastructure-related companies captured the bulk of third-quarter funding. Launch and space-access companies raised $16.4 billion across 120 deals, while satellite communications, Earth observation, and other service companies raised $4 billion. Major rounds during the quarter included Hadrian's $1.37 billion, Stoke Space's $1 billion, and K2 Space's $500 million.

Seraphim Space Vice President Lucas Bishop noted that capital is now chasing tangible evidence of commercial and institutional demand, rather than residual IPO enthusiasm. He said that as governments prioritize building domestic space capabilities, defense and sovereign demand are increasingly underpinning investment in launch, manufacturing, and orbital infrastructure.

The SpaceX siphoning effect: A hidden risk behind the primary-market boom

On June 12, SpaceX listed on the Nasdaq, surging more than 19% on its first day to a market capitalization of $2.1 trillion, making it the sixth-largest U.S. company. Yet on that same day, U.S. space-related stocks fell across the board: Virgin Galactic dropped more than 25%, while Intuitive Machines and Rocket Lab each fell over 8%.

SpaceX is no longer simply a rocket launch company. Its business spans three major segments — rocket launches, Starlink, and AI — and it handles more than 80% of the world's orbital payload deliveries. The "siphoning effect" created by this dominant position is accelerating the concentration of primary-market capital toward top-tier players, while small and mid-cap publicly listed space companies face pressure from capital and attention being drained away.

Bishop said many publicly listed space companies remain loss-making, and SpaceX's scale and visibility may be drawing investor attention away from smaller listed peers. SpaceX posted a full-year net loss of $4.937 billion in 2025 and an even larger $4.2 billion loss in the first quarter of 2026, underscoring that industry fundamentals still face serious tests.

Full-year outlook: First-ever $100 billion within reach, China a key variable

Space Capital, another early-stage venture firm, observed the third quarter from a longer time horizon in its own report. The firm has tracked space investment data since 2017. Its CEO Chad Anderson said: "We all thought 2021 was a crazy market, but compared to now, that year was just a blip."

Space Capital projects that, driven by SpaceX's record $85.7 billion IPO, defense spending, and space infrastructure buildout, global commercial space private funding in 2026 could top $100 billion for the first time in history. The first three quarters have already totaled $92.5 billion, with $22.2 billion flowing in during the third quarter alone. Pure-play launch companies were the most sought-after, with 58 rounds raising a combined $7.8 billion — a record for that sub-segment.

Geographically, North America accounted for roughly 70% of global funding year-to-date. China posted a quarterly high of $3.3 billion across 49 deals in the third quarter. More notably, Chinese space infrastructure funding in the first three quarters has already reached 2.7 times the full-year 2025 total, driven primarily by outsized rounds from commercial satellite manufacturers.

Corresponding developments within China have been intense. In February, iSpace completed a CNY 5.037 billion (approximately NT$24 billion) Series D++ round, setting a new record for a single round by a Chinese private rocket company, followed in August by the first closing of a Series E round of nearly CNY 1 billion. Arrowhead Technology has raised more than CNY 2.3 billion cumulatively over the past six months. LandSpace, CAS Space, Space Pioneer, and Galactic Energy are also queuing for IPOs.

Anderson pointed out that this funding boom beyond SpaceX stems partly from SpaceX's July decision to stop accepting rideshare launch bookings beyond 2028, with capacity prioritized for V3 Starlink deployment and Starship missions. "Launch scarcity" is forcing the market to find a number two, which is how Stoke and Blue Origin landed their mega-rounds. He described it as "the best thing to happen to the launch industry in a decade — this is how the number two, three, and four players get created."

The scissor gap: A tug-of-war between valuation and reality

Seraphim expects funding to moderate from the third quarter's exceptional highs, but to remain above historical norms as more companies enter growth and scaling phases. Against a backdrop of geopolitically driven sovereign satellite and missile-defense spending, and the accelerating convergence of AI and space hardware, space infrastructure is transitioning from concept to strategic asset.

Yet the "scissor gap" between the primary market's exuberant narrative and the secondary market's valuation digestion may become the industry's core tension for some time. Anderson warned that some companies currently raising money have built their entire business models on the assumption that "Starship will eventually open up capacity." The mismatch between high valuations and first-launch timelines is a widespread hidden risk — Blue Origin's New Glenn failure in May being the most recent example.

For Chinese companies, the structure is similar but the trajectory differs. Constrained by dual-use export controls, Chinese rockets are unlikely in the near term to directly capture third-party launch orders spilling over from SpaceX. The realistic opportunities lie more with sovereign constellation customers in the Global South and the Middle East, as well as exports of satellite manufacturing and ground equipment. Valuations of Chinese rocket companies are likewise built on the assumption that "Guowang and Qianfan constellation deployment density will continue." If the deployment cadence shifts, the valuation anchor will loosen.

Space computing has also emerged as a red-hot new frontier. Elon Musk announced that SpaceX will build the world's first space-based AI data center cluster, targeting 1 terawatt of AI compute deployment per year. Global space startup investment reached $55.3 billion in 2025, and the first quarter of 2026 alone saw a record $36 billion — evidence that this wave of space infrastructure investment is still accelerating.
